claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater plastic strain than pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing-component conditions.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater toughness than pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing-component conditions.
Equimolar mixing in WTaTiVZr induces substantial local atomic-scale lattice distortions.
The local lattice distortions in WTaTiVZr alter dislocation-core structures.
The altered dislocation-core structures favor edge-dislocation mobility in WTaTiVZr.
Plastic deformation in pure tungsten is predominantly governed by screw-dislocation motion under the proposed conditions.
Local lattice distortions in WTaTiVZr reduce the energy barrier for edge-dislocation motion.
Enhanced edge-dislocation mobility permits easier dislocation glide and greater plastic deformation in WTaTiVZr.
Easier glide and greater plastic deformation enhance the toughness of WTaTiVZr relative to pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit a higher density of mobile edge dislocations than pure tungsten during high-temperature deformation.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater ductility and deformation-energy absorption than pure tungsten.
Pure tungsten is an established plasma-facing material and therefore provides a service-relevant baseline.
Plasma-facing reactor service involves high temperature, high heat flux, and intense high-energy-neutron flux.
The proposed mechanism is particularly applicable above approximately 1000 K under high heat flux and irradiation.
The governing dislocation mechanism may differ at lower temperatures.
Irradiation-induced defects may modulate dislocation behavior and mechanical outcomes in WTaTiVZr.
Using WTaTiVZr and pure-tungsten specimens with comparable grain sizes and testing them under identical conditions controls major microstructural and environmental confounders.
Failure to observe both increased edge-dislocation activity and improved plastic strain or toughness in WTaTiVZr relative to pure tungsten would falsify the proposed mechanism.
